Sideeye finds out what your program leaves on disk when it dies at the worst possible moment. Declare an invariant — *"if this operation said it succeeded, this must still hold after a restart"* — and Sideeye kills your process before each state-changing operation, one crash world each, and brings back the earliest failing one as a replayable case. `sideeye demo`, trimmed, checked line by line in CI: ``` FAIL 1 of 6 explored worlds violated an invariant invariant built-in atomicity, and the checker earliest crash point 5 of 5 after unlink(…/state/key.json) before rename(…/state/key.json.tmp) path key.json observed present before and after the operation, but gone from the crashed state explored 6 worlds (crash points 5 + 1 baseline) checker falsified before the run (corrupted state -> check failed); ran in 6 world(s) case …/work/cases/000001.json not tested power loss, torn writes, concurrent processes ``` Counterexamples found: RuboCop, ImageMagick, the AWS CLI, [more](docs/found.md) — [four fixes](docs/case-studies.md). A target Sideeye cannot fully observe is UNKNOWN, never a silent PASS — except unrecorded writes under a directory a recorded `rename` moved in from outside, counted as `paths_attributed_to_rename` in every JSON report ([why](DESIGN.md#the-one-named-exception-a-directory-renamed-in-from-outside)). ## Installation Runs on macOS 14+ (Apple silicon) and Linux glibc (x86_64, aarch64): Homebrew, or a [release](https://github.com/yottayoshida/sideeye/releases) tarball run where you unpack it. Other platforms, building from source: [docs/cli.md](docs/cli.md#platforms). ``` $ brew install yottayoshida/tap/sideeye $ tar xzf sideeye-v1.13.0-aarch64-macos.tar.gz && cd sideeye-v1.13.0-aarch64-macos $ ./sideeye version ``` ## Usage ``` $ sideeye demo $ sideeye preflight --state --operation "" $ sideeye explore --config sideeye.toml --oracle /usr/bin/strace $ sideeye explore --config sideeye.toml --allow-unverified ``` - **`demo`** — sixty seconds, no compiler; one directory left under `$TMPDIR` (or `/tmp`) with the saved case. Exit 1, the bug found, is success. - **`preflight`** — can Sideeye watch your tool? One observed run: `recording accepted`, or a refusal naming the detector. - **`explore`** — the real thing; the define in one file: ```toml [world] state = "./state" # your tool's state [define] cwd = "." # relative arguments resolve here setup = "mytool init" operation = "mytool rotate-key" # the shim is inserted into this one, not into setup or check check = "./check.sh" # exit 0 = invariant holds ``` `operation` is the one command the shim is inserted into; command strings split on spaces, no quoting. `--oracle` is a second witness, the kernel's account (Linux; on macOS, `--oracle-fs-usage`); without one, PASS needs `--allow-unverified`, and the report says so. `--shim` names the shim when it is not beside the binary; `--work` moves the scratch directory. Exit codes: **0 PASS, 1 FAIL, 2 UNKNOWN, 3 SETUP ERROR**. A FAIL saves a replayable case, and `sideeye evidence ` renders it for an issue tracker. Run `explore --config` in CI ([docs/ci-quickstart.md](docs/ci-quickstart.md)). For agents there is `sideeye mcp`, and three skills (`npx skills@1.7.1 add yottayoshida/sideeye`): [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md). ## Writing the check The check, like the setup, receives the state directory in `$SIDEEYE_STATE_DIR`. This one cross-examines the tool's own diagnostic; the violation is the claim and the observable truth disagreeing: ```sh claim=$("$TOY" doctor 2>/dev/null) || claim="unhealthy" "$TOY" load-key >/dev/null 2>&1 && reality="loadable" || reality="unloadable" case "$claim:$reality" in healthy:loadable | unhealthy:unloadable) exit 0 ;; *) echo "doctor says '$claim' but the key is $reality" >&2; exit 1 ;; esac ``` Sideeye refuses to trust a checker it has not seen fail: it corrupts the state first. A checker that cannot fail makes the run UNKNOWN, not PASS; so does an exploration in which no world could have failed ([conditions](docs/report-schema.md)). ## What the target has to be Sideeye refuses to guess: outside these limits the verdict is UNKNOWN, naming the detector. Reasons: [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md#known-constraints-declared-not-hidden). - **Dynamically linked**, reaching files through libc; static only under `--observe supervised` (Linux). Hardened runtimes are refused. Threads are judged where a creation or a join the shim saw orders their writes. - **Under `--observe syscalls`, a process whose `SIGSYS` is blocked or reset dies at its first state-changing call** — an `exec`'d image the shim cannot reach, a `posix_spawn` child. - **Byte-repeatable writes** (`preflight --twice` checks), **state in one directory**, **a clean run exits its declared success status**. - **Other processes take turns with the state**, and every writing child is reaped; a process boundary needs Linux's `--oracle`, and one that leaves its process group is judged only where the engine can hold the run in a cgroup (Linux) — otherwise UNKNOWN. - **On macOS, a framework Python's `bin/python3` is a launcher**; Sideeye refuses it and names the interpreter to run instead. No language model decides a verdict; a PASS is a search record naming what was *not* tested. ## Documentation [docs/faq.md](docs/faq.md) · [docs/cli.md](docs/cli.md) · [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md) · [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) · [docs/report-schema.md](docs/report-schema.md) · [docs/target-classes.md](docs/target-classes.md) · [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) · [docs/](docs/) ## License [MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or [Apache-2.0](LICENSE-APACHE), at your option. # The CLI in full The README carries the shortest path to a first verdict. On Alpine the shim entered the demo's toy in both builds — v1.10.0's compiled with Alpine's `cc`, main's (at `ca6bdbdf`) carried in the engine — where ADR 0101 expected a static toy the shim could not enter. ## Installing without Homebrew Take the tarball for your platform from [Releases](https://github.com/yottayoshida/sideeye/releases). Sideeye ships as a binary **and** a shim library, and it looks for the shim beside **itself** — the binary's own canonical path, never the working directory — before `../lib`, so an untarred release runs from anywhere and needs no `--shim` unless you have separated the two files. That search declines a candidate it cannot attribute (a symlink, or a file someone else owns), so an install directory that is not yours alone is refused by name rather than trusted: ``` $ tar xzf sideeye-v1.13.0-aarch64-macos.tar.gz && cd sideeye-v1.13.0-aarch64-macos $ ./sideeye version ``` Each release asset carries a sha256 GitHub computed when it was uploaded, so checking a download needs nothing published beside it (on Linux, `sha256sum` in place of `shasum -a 256`): ``` $ gh api repos/yottayoshida/sideeye/releases/tags/v1.13.0 --jq '.assets[] | "\(.digest) \(.name)"' $ shasum -a 256 sideeye-v1.13.0-aarch64-macos.tar.gz ``` The digest reads `sha256:`; compare the hex. What this establishes is that the bytes are the ones GitHub holds — not who produced them: the digest and the release are the same account's word, and a checksum file published in the same release would be too. Or build from source with Zig 0.16.0: `zig build` — binaries land in `zig-out/bin` and `zig-out/lib`, which is the same shape. Whether a newer Zig builds it is checked weekly by [`zig-ahead.yml`](../.github/workflows/zig-ahead.yml), and the breakages already known are listed in [`spike/zig-ahead-known.tsv`](../spike/zig-ahead-known.tsv). ## Usage Three commands, in the order you will meet them. **1. The tool is built into the binary, so no compiler is needed (#715). The directory is named on the demo's first line and left in place, so the case it saves can be replayed; delete it when you are done. Exit 1 — the planted bug found — is success, which makes the demo double as a smoke test of the binary + shim pair. **2. `spike/check.sh`, the acceptance toy's checker (the README quotes part of it): run the tool's `doctor`, run the operation that depends on the same state, and require the two to **agree** — healthy things must work, unhealthy things must say so. #!/bin/sh
# The L2 checker: cross-examine the diagnostic command against reality.
#
# The invariant is not "the key is readable" — a target is allowed to be broken as
# long as it says so. The invariant is that `doctor`'s claim and the observable truth
# agree. Both directions are violations: claiming health while the key cannot be read,
# and claiming trouble while it can.
#
# Runs after a restart, in a fresh process, exactly as DESIGN §12 requires. Exit 0
# means the invariant holds.
#
# Environment:
#   TOY    path to the toy binary
#   TOY_STATE  state directory (passed through to the toy)

set -u

: "${TOY:?check.sh needs TOY to point at the binary under test}"

if claim=$("$TOY" doctor 2>/dev/null); then
    :
else
    claim="unhealthy"
fi

if "$TOY" load-key >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    reality="loadable"
else
    reality="unloadable"
fi

case "$claim:$reality" in
    healthy:loadable)     exit 0 ;;
    unhealthy:unloadable) exit 0 ;;
    *)
        echo "doctor says '$claim' but the key is $reality" >&2
        exit 1
        ;;
esac
```

## Recipe 2 — the non-destruction form

`spike/loop-closure-timew/define/check.sh`, the checker behind the timewarrior finding — its one canonical text, beside `setup.sh` and `operation`; the scripts that stage or replay the define (`stage.sh`, `dogfood-timew-replay.sh`) copy the checker and setup and read the operation from there rather than carrying their own, and the frozen v0.4 recipe `spike/dogfood-timew.sh` keeps a copy the unknown-rate corpus pins, a record rather than a consumer (#65): after `timew undo`, the export must have removed *either nothing or exactly the newest interval*. The first draft demanded that undo always remove something — which condemns a correct recovery along with the bug, because a crash may have beaten the intent's commit; `spike/dogfood-timew.sh` carries that rationale beside the checker text. The admission is written down too: this form deliberately allows an undo that always no-ops, so the loop-closure apparatus scores a fix that *lobotomizes* the feature as a failure on a separate gate — declared before the run, not discovered after (`BUILDLOG.md`). One limit the code below makes visible and the sentence above does not: the comparison is over the *set* of interval keys, so it is blind to multiplicity — an undo that left a duplicate of an interval already present would add no new key and pass. The claim the checker actually carries is about which keys appear and disappear, not how many times each does.

#!/bin/sh
# The declared invariant (L2 checker), non-destruction form: undo must remove either
# nothing or exactly the interval timew's own export names as most recent — never an
# older committed interval, and it must not invent intervals. Removing nothing is
# allowed because a crash may have beaten the intent's commit.
#
# This file is the one canonical text of the checker (#65). The scripts that stage or
# replay the define copy it from here; none carries its own. The frozen v0.4 recipe,
# whose bytes the unknown-rate corpus pins, is a record rather than a consumer.
set -eu
before=$(timew export) || exit 1
timew undo >/dev/null || exit 1
after=$(timew export) || exit 1
BEFORE="$before" AFTER="$after" python3 - <<'PY'
import json, os, sys

def key(iv):
    return (iv["start"], iv.get("end", ""), ",".join(iv.get("tags", [])))

before = json.loads(os.environ["BEFORE"])
after = json.loads(os.environ["AFTER"])
if not before:
    print("export was empty before undo: the seeded interval is gone", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)
newest = min(before, key=lambda iv: iv["id"])  # id 1 is timew's own "most recent"
b = sorted(key(iv) for iv in before)
a = sorted(key(iv) for iv in after)
added = [k for k in a if k not in b]
removed = [k for k in b if k not in a]
if added:
    print("undo added intervals:", added, file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)
if removed not in ([], [key(newest)]):
    print("undo removed the wrong change: timew's own export named", key(newest),
          "as most recent, but undo removed", removed, file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)
PY

## Recipe 5 — all or none, across files

`spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/apparatus/defines/useradd/check.sh`, the checker behind the 2026-10-14 mechanisms run's `useradd` FAIL (#861). `useradd` replaces `passwd`, `shadow`, `group` and `gshadow` one after another, each whole through a temporary and a rename, so a kill between two of them leaves every file intact and the four contradicting each other — and the built-in atomicity form, which judges each file on its own (`group` and `gshadow` old-or-new; `passwd` and `shadow` by their history form, which does not judge an appended tail), has nothing to say. Leg c counts the user across all four files and accepts four or none. Of the 71 explored worlds, 21 FAILed, and leg c was red in all 21; `pwck` (leg a) was red too in 7 of them and `grpck` (leg b) in another 7, and in the remaining 7 leg c alone saw it — which is why the count, not the tools' own consistency checks, is the leg to copy.

The checker also runs the recovery a user would run — the same `useradd` again, its "already exists" accepted — before it judges, and prints the legs before that too. ## Failure patterns, each with the run that taught it

- **A broken state the recovery heals is no red.** A checker that runs the tool's recovery first has to be shown broken states the recovery cannot repair. In the 2026-10-14 mechanisms run, update-alternatives' first broken state for leg b pointed the link under its alternatives directory at the other editor; the checker's recovery, the same `--install`, put the link back, and the checker passed it — correctly — so the control said nothing about leg b until the broken state was one `--install` leaves alone (the generic link replaced by a plain file). The first form is recorded in prose, not in a transcript (`spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/SELECTION.md`, and the comment in `spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/apparatus/defines/alternatives/legs.sh`); the run's one-broken-state-per-leg controls are `spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/apparatus/controls.sh`, with their output in `spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/transcripts/controls.txt`.
- **Exit-0-on-unreadable.** todoman's `list` prints a traceback and exits 0 — it answers "nothing wrong" precisely when it could not look. The falsification gate refused it: the first real checker rejected as unfalsifiable, as opposed to a synthetic `/bin/true` (`BUILDLOG.md`, the todoman entry). The committed fix is a strict wrapper — exit 0 AND no error text in the output (`spike/dogfood-todoman.sh`).
- **Demanding destruction.** A checker that requires the operation to have visibly happened condemns correct crash recovery along with the bug (recipe 2). Allow the no-op; let a separate gate judge whether a fix gutted the feature.
- **Counting lines when you mean occurrences.** `grep -c` counts lines; devtodo rewrites its whole store onto one XML line, so a duplicated note still counted as 1. `spike/assisted/devtodo/ops/check.sh` counts occurrences instead (`grep -o` piped to a line count) and records the review finding that caught it.
- **Asserting what you did not observe.** The general shape behind all of the above: the claim and the observable truth must agree. Every blind-campaign checker under `spike/blind-hunt/`, `spike/blind-hunt2/` and `spike/blind-hunt3/` ships with a red suite beside it proving each leg can individually fail — the cheapest way to know a checker is load-bearing.
- **A scratch file is not a counterexample — and only a checker knows which is which.** git commit reaches a full verdict and FAILs at one crash point: COMMIT_EDITMSG, opened with truncation before the message is written, torn to empty by a kill in that window. It is not a git bug — git rewrites the file on the next commit and never reads a torn one — and L0 has no way to know a file is scratch (DESIGN §12's per-file atomicity exempts no file *by its role* — a scratch file is judged like any other). The taught fix: a target with scratch files needs a checker carrying the *real* integrity claim — the same run with `git fsck --connectivity-only` as the checker accepted every crash world, because git's actual durability (objects, refs, index) held in all of them. # Apparatus: declaring what a deterministic run depends on

A target that stamps the clock, draws random ids or numbers its files from an
inode is refused at the baseline (`baseline_violates_invariant`, naming the
path — see "Byte-repeatable writes" in the README's limits). The cohorts that
measured such targets got past the wall by pinning the source of variation
outside the target: a faked clock, a seeded `os.urandom`, a stand-in compiler.
Every one of those lived in a launcher script or in `setup`, and the committed
define said nothing about it.

`[define] apparatus` is where the define says it (ADR 0041). Sideeye applies
none of it. After `setup` and before the first snapshot it checks that every
entry it can check is present in the environment the operation will inherit,
and refuses the run as SETUP ERROR — naming the entry and what it looked at —
when one is not. The report carries the list as declared in `apparatus`, and
the entries it could not check in `apparatus_unchecked`.

```toml
[define]
setup     = "./pins/setup.sh"      # generates sitecustomize.py, plants the flag file
operation = "borg create ::a /src"
apparatus = [
  "env:FAKETIME=@2024-01-01 00:00:00",
  "preload:libfaketime",
  "pythonpath:sitecustomize.py",
  "note:borg's --no-cache-sync is passed on the command line",
]
```

(The example spans lines for reading; the accepted form is one `[` ... `]`
line, the same as the commands' argv form.)

| entry | what is checked | where the device is set |
|---|---|---|
| `env:NAME` | `NAME` is set in the environment the operation inherits | the launcher, or the shell |
| `env:NAME=VALUE` | set, and equal to `VALUE` — for devices whose value *is* the device (`PAPIS_NP=0`, `FAKETIME=...`) | same |
| `preload:LIB` | a line of `/etc/ld.so.preload` names a library whose basename starts with `LIB` | the launcher writes the line (needs root). Linux only |
| `pythonpath:FILE` | some entry of `PYTHONPATH` has `FILE` directly under it. Existence only: the content is not judged | `setup` generates the file; the launcher exports `PYTHONPATH` |
| `note:TEXT` | nothing — carried, listed as unchecked | wherever it lives (an hgrc line, a container's seccomp profile, a pin applied inside the operation's own command line) |

## The one thing to know about `preload:`

**Never through `LD_PRELOAD`.** Sideeye replaces `LD_PRELOAD` with its own
shim for every child it spawns (that is how it records the operation), so a
library the launcher put there does not reach the operation — and it would be
a silent absence: the run records, the clock is real, the baseline refuses
without saying why. If `LD_PRELOAD` does name the library and
`/etc/ld.so.preload` does not, the refusal says exactly that.

`/etc/ld.so.preload` is global. A library named there rides on **every**
process on the machine for the duration, the engine's own `/bin/sh -c`
included (the shape that once made every world report
`child_process_detected`) and, under `--oracle`, on `strace`'s children. The
cohorts did this inside a container, and that is the recipe: pin in a
container, name the pin in the define. A pid pin has the same global reach and
no per-target form Sideeye can see, which is why cohort 4's `pin-getpid.c` was
applied inside the operation's command line and is declared as a `note:`.

On macOS there is no global preload file and Sideeye owns
`DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`; a define with a `preload:` entry is refused there as
unsatisfiable.

## What the check does not prove

- `pythonpath:` proves the file exists under some entry, not that it is the
  file the define meant, nor that Python will import it first.
- `env:NAME` without a value proves presence, not that the value is the one
  the run needs; write the value when the value is the device.
- The checker's environment is the define's business. A checker may drop a
  device on purpose (cohort 3's cargo-r2 unsets `RUSTC` to compare against the
  real compiler); the check is about the operation's environment only.
- The saved case does not carry the declaration. A replay without the
  apparatus is not silent — the baseline does not repeat the recorded bytes
  and the refusal names the path — but the case file itself does not say
  which device was missing.

Threads are judged where a creation or a join the shim saw orders their writes. 85 - **Under `--observe syscalls`, a process whose `SIGSYS` is blocked or reset dies at its first state-changing call** — an `exec`'d image the shim cannot reach, a `posix_spawn` child. 86 - **Byte-repeatable writes** (`preflight --twice` checks), **state in one directory**, **a clean run exits its declared success status**. 87 - **Other processes take turns with the state**, and every writing child is reaped; a process boundary needs Linux's `--oracle`, and one that leaves its process group is judged only where the engine can hold the run in a cgroup (Linux) — otherwise UNKNOWN. 88 - **On macOS, a framework Python's `bin/python3` is a launcher**; Sideeye refuses it and names the interpreter to run instead. 89 90 No language model decides a verdict; a PASS is a search record naming what was *not* tested. 91 92 ## Documentation 93 94 [docs/faq.md](docs/faq.md) · [docs/cli.md](docs/cli.md) · [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md) · [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) · [docs/report-schema.md](docs/report-schema.md) · [docs/target-classes.md](docs/target-classes.md) · [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) · [docs/](docs/) 95 96 ## License 97 98 [MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or [Apache-2.0](LICENSE-APACHE), at your option. 99 # The CLI in full 100 101 The README carries the shortest path to a first verdict. Sideeye ships as a binary **and** a shim library, and it looks for the shim beside **itself** — the binary's own canonical path, never the working directory — before `../lib`, so an untarred release runs from anywhere and needs no `--shim` unless you have separated the two files. That search declines a candidate it cannot attribute (a symlink, or a file someone else owns), so an install directory that is not yours alone is refused by name rather than trusted: 134 135 ``` 136 $ tar xzf sideeye-v1.13.0-aarch64-macos.tar.gz && cd sideeye-v1.13.0-aarch64-macos 137 $ ./sideeye version 138 ``` 139 140 Each release asset carries a sha256 GitHub computed when it was uploaded, so checking a download needs nothing published beside it (on Linux, `sha256sum` in place of `shasum -a 256`): 141 142 ``` 143 $ gh api repos/yottayoshida/sideeye/releases/tags/v1.13.0 --jq '.assets[] | "\(.digest) \(.name)"' 144 $ shasum -a 256 sideeye-v1.13.0-aarch64-macos.tar.gz 145 ``` 146 147 The digest reads `sha256:`; compare the hex. What this establishes is that the bytes are the ones GitHub holds — not who produced them: the digest and the release are the same account's word, and a checksum file published in the same release would be too. 148 149 Or build from source with Zig 0.16.0: `zig build` — binaries land in `zig-out/bin` and `zig-out/lib`, which is the same shape. Whether a newer Zig builds it is checked weekly by [`zig-ahead.yml`](../.github/workflows/zig-ahead.yml), and the breakages already known are listed in [`spike/zig-ahead-known.tsv`](../spike/zig-ahead-known.tsv). 150 151 ## Usage 152 153 Three commands, in the order you will meet them. 154 155 **1. See it work** — sixty seconds, nothing to install beyond Sideeye itself: 156 157 ``` 158 $ sideeye demo 159 ``` 160 161 The demo writes a small planted-bug tool into a new directory under `$TMPDIR` (or `/tmp`), explores it, and prints a real FAIL report. The tool is built into the binary, so no compiler is needed (#715). The directory is named on the demo's first line and left in place, so the case it saves can be replayed; delete it when you are done. Exit 1 — the planted bug found — is success, which makes the demo double as a smoke test of the binary + shim pair. 162 163 **2. Ask whether Sideeye can watch your tool** — before writing any config, and again once you have one: 164 165 ``` 166 $ sideeye preflight --state --operation "" 167 ``` 168 169 One observed run: either `recording accepted` (exit 0) or a refusal naming the same detector a real run would use (exit 2). It starts where explore's recording does: the state the setup left is snapshotted, emptied and rebuilt from the snapshot first (#815), so preflight rewrites the state directory too, and takes `--state-under`. An accepted run — under `--twice`, one whose two runs left the same bytes — ends with a `next` line, the `explore` command for the define it just accepted, ending in what explore on this platform takes: the second witness `--oracle ` on Linux; on macOS, where `--oracle` is refused, `--allow-unverified` — no second witness, the weaker claim, said so in the report — with `--oracle-fs-usage` named in the note above it as the witness macOS has (#702). 170 171 Once a `sideeye.toml` exists, the same question takes the toml itself, read as explore reads it: 172 173 ``` 174 $ sideeye preflight --config sideeye.toml 175 ``` 176 177 **Every define mistake listed below is refused by `sideeye preflight --config` before any crash world, by the same detector and in the same words `explore --config` uses** — one mistake per run, the first one met, as explore does (#704, ADR 0094): 178 179 - the toml does not parse: a syntax error, an unknown key, a value of the wrong shape; 180 - a `cwd`, `apparatus` or `scratch` entry that does not hold; 181 - a `state` that is not a directory; 182 - a `setup`, `operation` or `check` that cannot be started, as the Usage list below defines it; 183 - a `marker` the recording run does not print (`marker_never_observed`); 184 - an operation that changes nothing in the state directory, so there is no crash point (`nothing_could_fail`) — explore answers this in the same words when it is given `--oracle` or `--allow-unverified`, and answers the completeness gate first without either; 185 - for an operation with a crash point, a `check` with no command in it (`--check is empty`), or one declared against a state with nothing in it to corrupt (`checker_not_falsified`); 186 - in a toml with no `cwd`, run from another directory, a relative argument that is under the toml's directory and not where the commands ran — named, with `cwd = "."` as the line to add. 187 188 Neither the check nor a `[recovery]` is run: the report says each was declared, and a recovery that cannot be started moves no verdict in explore either (ADR 0072). What a world can do differently from the recording is not on the list: an operation that changes the state but nothing the verdict judges can still be refused `nothing_could_fail` by explore, which only a crash world shows. An accepted run's `next` line is `sideeye explore --config ''`, named in the directory its relative paths were resolved against (a toml that is a symlink keeps its own side); a toml read from `/dev/stdin`, from a shell's `<(…)`, or through a link into `/dev` or `/proc` gets a line saying to save it to a file first, and one whose name cannot be printed as typed a line saying to copy it to a file with a plain name. (zsh's `=(…)` is an ordinary temporary file and is named as one, though it is gone once the command ends.) 189 190 Add `--twice` and it observes the operation twice, each run from the rebuilt pre-state, the second at least two seconds after the first, and compares the two. Byte repeatability is a property of two runs — one observation structurally cannot see it, and a tool that rewrites a timestamp on every run passes everything else preflight asks and is refused only once a full define has been written and explored. Equal post-states: exit 0. Different: the differing paths are named and the command exits 1, which is the negative answer to the question `--twice` asked, not a FAIL verdict — preflight produces none. Under each path it names whose content differs, up to eight of them, a `bytes` line says where the two runs' bytes first differ (a byte offset counted from 0), how long the differing stretch is in each run — what is left once the bytes both runs share at the front and at the back are taken off, widened over shared bytes to a whole UTF-8 character where the first or last difference falls inside a valid one (the line then says where the stretch starts) — what kind of bytes it holds (decimal digits; hex digits, which takes a digit and a letter both; printable text, tabs, line ends and invisible format characters included; or how many bytes fall outside printable text), and quotes both stretches, each clipped at 48 bytes, with every byte outside printable text — tabs and line ends too — and every character that reorders or hides text on a terminal (the bidi controls, the zero-width and invisible marks, tag characters) spelled `\xNN` (#688): 191 192 ``` 193 difference nondet.txt (content differs) 194 bytes first differ at byte offset 4: first run "1", second run "2" — 1 and 1 byte(s) of 10 and 10, both decimal digits 195 ``` 196 197 The quoted bytes are in preflight's text output, and — when `--oracle` ran — in the oracle's capture in the work directory, since strace prints the start of what each write wrote; they are not in its `--json` document, which carries where, how long and what kind (below). So wherever the text output or the work directory is kept, a CI log or a committed transcript, those bytes of the state are kept with it. An exploration that refuses `baseline_violates_invariant` over the same difference says where, how long and what kind, and no byte of either stretch, because its message reaches the JSON report, the MCP answer and the reports people paste upstream — and a stretch two runs disagree on is exactly where a per-run token or secret sits. Neither names a cause; [docs/apparatus.md](apparatus.md#reading-a-byte-difference) maps the common shapes to `scratch` and `apparatus`. What it does not establish is that the target is deterministic: the comparison covers file bytes, entry kinds and symlink targets in the state directory (`--state`, or a toml's `[world] state` under `--config`), and two runs are not all runs. 198 199 With `--json `, preflight writes what it found as JSON (#717). A refusal or a stop is a report, `sideeye/report`, carrying the refusal the text shows — usually the one `explore` reaches on the same define, though not always (above: with no crash point and neither `--oracle` nor `--allow-unverified`, explore answers its completeness gate first). An accepted recording, or two runs that differ under `--twice`, is a document of its own, `sideeye/preflight`: the outcome, the account, the set of paths the built-in invariant judges, and under `--twice` each differing path with where, how long and what kind of bytes — never a byte of either run ([docs/report-schema.md](report-schema.md#preflights-document-preflight---json)). The exit code is the same as without the flag. 200 201 **3. Explore** — the real thing, with the whole define in one file. The first line is Linux's; the second is macOS's, where `--oracle` (strace) is refused: 202 203 ``` 204 $ sideeye explore --config sideeye.toml --oracle /usr/bin/strace 205 $ sideeye explore --config sideeye.toml --allow-unverified 206 ``` 207 208 ```toml 209 [world] 210 state = "./state" # the one directory your tool's state lives in 211 212 [define] 213 setup = "mytool init" 214 operation = "mytool rotate-key" # the shim is inserted into this one, not into setup or check 215 check = "./check.sh" # exit 0 = invariant holds; runs after crash + restart 216 marker = "Recorded" # optional: the operation's own success claim 217 expected_status = "3" # optional: the exit status that means "completed" (default "0") 218 cwd = "./repo" # optional: where the three commands run (default: sideeye's own cwd) 219 apparatus = ["env:FAKETIME=@2024-01-01 00:00:00", "preload:libfaketime"] # optional: what the operation's environment must carry 220 scratch = ["COMMIT_EDITMSG", ".hg/wcache"] # optional: paths under state the built-in invariants leave alone 221 222 [recovery] # optional: the tool's own recovery, run against each saved FAIL 223 command = "mytool repair" # the string form only 224 check = "./check-repaired.sh" 225 ``` 226 227 - The same define works as flags: `--state` / `--setup` / `--operation` / `--check` / `--marker` / `--expect-status` / `--cwd` / `--apparatus` (repeatable) / `--scratch` (repeatable). `operation` is **the one command the shim is inserted into**; `setup` and `check` are ordinary commands and may be scripts. What that means for a `#!` script: the kernel hands execution to the interpreter, so the insertion has to reach *that* image rather than the file you named. Whether it can is a property of the interpreter and of the machine — a statically linked one takes no insertion anywhere, and on macOS a platform binary such as `/bin/sh` may have the variable stripped before it starts — so the same define can reach a verdict on one machine and refuse with `no_shim_marker` on another. Naming an executable image directly takes the question away. 228 - **A setup, operation or check that cannot be started is a SETUP ERROR (exit 3), raised before it runs**, naming the command, the file and which of these it is: the file is missing, is not a regular file, may not be executed by this user (a script needs its execute bit — Sideeye runs `./check.sh`, not `sh check.sh` — or a noexec mount or an ACL denies it), or could not be examined; the `#!` interpreter that file names is one of those; or a bare name has no executable file on `PATH`. A bare name is refused only when every file of that name on `PATH` fails this way, because execvp moves on to the next one. The setup is asked about before it runs, and that refusal leaves nothing on disk; the operation and the check after the setup has run, so a setup may build or write them — but a checker the operation itself would create is refused, so write it in `setup`. Not judged, and still arriving as whatever status the failed exec leaves: a bare name when `PATH` is unset (the libcs' default lists differ), a script this user can execute but not read, a `#!` line longer than 256 bytes, a relative interpreter, an `env` line with a flag, a second word, or a name holding `/` or `=`, a second level of `env` (the file `env` finds has a broken `#!` of its own), an executable whose dynamic loader is missing (a glibc binary on Alpine), an image built for another CPU, and a file that disappears between the question and the spawn. Under `--observe supervised` and `--oracle` the operation is launched from the first file of that name on `PATH` with no fallback, so a broken first file with a working one behind it passes the question and fails at the spawn. The `[recovery]` commands are not asked about — a recovery changes no verdict and no exit code, so one that cannot start shows as `recovery.result` `unknown` (#701, ADR 0092). 229 - `cwd` is where setup, operation and checker run — **a tool that only works inside its own project (git, most build tools) needs one**, and without it the commands run in Sideeye's own directory. For a tool that refuses to run outside its project that is usually `recording_run_failed`, with the exit status and no cause — or `setup_failed` when `setup` needs the directory too, whose one-line text carries no `cwd` line (the JSON does). The quiet case is worse: a tool that walks up the tree to find its project, as git does, can find a *different* one above Sideeye's directory and succeed there, and nothing refuses. Every report produced after the `cwd` is resolved says which directory the commands ran in: `command_cwd` in the JSON and a `cwd` line in the text — on an UNKNOWN under `next`, in the verdict blocks, and in `preflight`'s report, whose `next` hint carries the `--cwd` it was given — with `(none declared: Sideeye's own)` when nothing was declared (#647). For a define read from a toml that declares no `cwd`, run from a directory other than the toml's, a refusal also says what it saw when the command that failed carries an argument present under the toml's directory and absent where it ran — or, for a file it is about to create, a directory above that file that is — `./state is under the toml's directory /proj and not under /home/u, where the commands ran` — and names `cwd = "."` as the line to add: in `next_step` on `recording_run_failed` (an exit status nobody declared, or no normal exit), `marker_never_observed`, `nothing_could_fail` when there was no crash point (an operation that found nothing to do where it ran), `checker_not_falsified` when the checker accepted the corrupted state, `checker_rejects_initial_state` when it rejected the state the define starts from, and `baseline_violates_invariant`'s checker layer; in the sentence itself on `setup_failed` when the setup exited non-zero, and wherever `--observe syscalls` keeps its own step (#700, ADR 0093). Not asked for a config read through a link or a pipe (`/dev/stdin`). It sees nothing when the command finds a different file where it ran and succeeds, or writes outside the state directory through an argument that names nothing either side — which is why the README's toml example declares `cwd = "."`. In a `sideeye.toml` a relative `cwd` resolves against **the toml's own directory**, not against where Sideeye was started and not against the project's root unless the toml sits there; given as the `--cwd` flag it resolves, like any path on the command line, against the directory Sideeye was started in. **It is resolved and checked before the state directory is made**, so that a define naming a directory that is not there refuses before anything on disk has moved — which means **a `cwd` that only your own `setup` creates is not there yet when it is checked**: the run refuses as a SETUP ERROR (`the declared cwd could not be resolved`) before setup runs. (Left over from an earlier run it would resolve, which is worse — the define would work on one machine and not on a clean one.) Build such a directory before Sideeye starts — in CI, in the step before the one that runs it. 230 - `apparatus` names the devices a deterministic run depends on — a faked clock, a pinned `os.urandom`, a stand-in compiler — so the define is the whole question and the report says what it ran under. Sideeye applies none of it; after `setup` it checks that each `env:`, `preload:` (a line of `/etc/ld.so.preload`) and `pythonpath:` entry is present in the environment the operation inherits and refuses the run as SETUP ERROR when one is not. `note:` entries are carried unchecked. Recipes and the one thing to know about global preloads: [docs/apparatus.md](apparatus.md). 231 - `scratch` names the paths under `state` that nobody depends on — git's `COMMIT_EDITMSG`, a tool's own cache — each entry covering the path itself and everything beneath it. The built-in invariants judge none of them, in no world: not their bytes, not their presence, whether the recording had them before, after, or both, so a torn scratch file no longer decides the verdict and a scratch file whose bytes differ between two clean runs no longer refuses the run. The price is paid in the open: the report carries the declaration verbatim, its `atomicity` line says how many recorded paths the declaration matched, `not tested` names it, and the saved case carries it (a define that declared everything reads `0 path(s) judged pre-or-post` — and, with no checker to judge the worlds instead (a marker has nothing to judge there either), is refused `nothing_could_fail`, because no world in it could have failed (ADR 0091)). What scratch does not silence: a state that changed with no operation recorded, a child the engine could not account for, an entry kind or a file size the snapshot refuses, a tree still being written when it is sampled twice — those are about what the engine observed, not about what is durable. And a checker is still the only thing that says the state is *correct*; scratch only stops the built-in layers from saying it is not (ADR 0043). 232 - `[recovery]` (or `--recovery` with `--recovery-check`) asks a second question about each FAIL: what does the tool's own recovery do to the state the crash left? **Declaring a recovery changes no verdict and no exit code; for each saved FAIL world it adds what the tool's own recovery did when handed that world's crash state — its names, kinds, contents and permission bits (a directory with its owner's bits added), not its timestamps, owners, or set-id and sticky bits.** After the exploration has decided its verdict, and only when there is a FAIL, the recovery checker is first shown a state whose every file holds distinct junk and must reject it, and then the completed, uncrashed state with `command` run on it, and must accept what that leaves; then, for the earliest exhibit and the checker exhibit (once if they are one world), the crash state is rebuilt in `state`, `command` runs, the state is sampled twice to see it has stopped changing, and `check` judges it. The report's `earliest.recovery` and `checker_earliest.recovery` say `pass`, `fail` or `unknown` with the time taken, the `recovery` line says what the result rests on, and the evidence bundle carries the result. `fail` means the recovery ran, ended and was rejected; a recovery that could not be started, exited 125, 126 or 127 (the codes the engine's own child uses before exec), overran `--world-timeout`, left something still writing or running where its cgroup could not stop it, or whose checker accepted the junk or rejected the completed state is `unknown`, never `fail`. Declare an invariant — *"if this operation said it succeeded, this must still hold after a restart"* — and Sideeye kills your process before each state-changing operation, one crash world each, and brings back the earliest failing one as a replayable case. `sideeye demo`, trimmed, checked line by line in CI: ``` FAIL 1 of 6 explored worlds violated an invariant invariant built-in atomicity, and the checker earliest crash point 5 of 5 after unlink(…/state/key.json) before rename(…/state/key.json.tmp) path key.json observed present before and after the operation, but gone from the crashed state explored 6 worlds (crash points 5 + 1 baseline) checker falsified before the run (corrupted state -> check failed); ran in 6 world(s) case …/work/cases/000001.json not tested power loss, torn writes, concurrent processes ``` Counterexamples found: RuboCop, ImageMagick, the AWS CLI, [more](docs/found.md) — [four fixes](docs/case-studies.md). A target Sideeye cannot fully observe is UNKNOWN, never a silent PASS — except unrecorded writes under a directory a recorded `rename` moved in from outside, counted as `paths_attributed_to_rename` in every JSON report ([why](DESIGN.md#the-one-named-exception-a-directory-renamed-in-from-outside)). ## Installation Runs on macOS 14+ (Apple silicon) and Linux glibc (x86_64, aarch64): Homebrew, or a [release](https://github.com/yottayoshida/sideeye/releases) tarball run where you unpack it. Other platforms, building from source: [docs/cli.md](docs/cli.md#platforms). ``` $ brew install yottayoshida/tap/sideeye $ tar xzf sideeye-v1.13.0-aarch64-macos.tar.gz && cd sideeye-v1.13.0-aarch64-macos $ ./sideeye version ``` ## Usage ``` $ sideeye demo $ sideeye preflight --state --operation "" $ sideeye explore --config sideeye.toml --oracle /usr/bin/strace $ sideeye explore --config sideeye.toml --allow-unverified ``` - **`demo`** — sixty seconds, no compiler; one directory left under `$TMPDIR` (or `/tmp`) with the saved case. Exit 1, the bug found, is success. - **`preflight`** — can Sideeye watch your tool? One observed run: `recording accepted`, or a refusal naming the detector. - **`explore`** — the real thing; the define in one file: ```toml [world] state = "./state" # your tool's state [define] cwd = "." # relative arguments resolve here setup = "mytool init" operation = "mytool rotate-key" # the shim is inserted into this one, not into setup or check check = "./check.sh" # exit 0 = invariant holds ``` `operation` is the one command the shim is inserted into; command strings split on spaces, no quoting. `--oracle` is a second witness, the kernel's account (Linux; on macOS, `--oracle-fs-usage`); without one, PASS needs `--allow-unverified`, and the report says so. `--shim` names the shim when it is not beside the binary; `--work` moves the scratch directory. Exit codes: **0 PASS, 1 FAIL, 2 UNKNOWN, 3 SETUP ERROR**. A FAIL saves a replayable case, and `sideeye evidence ` renders it for an issue tracker. Run `explore --config` in CI ([docs/ci-quickstart.md](docs/ci-quickstart.md)). For agents there is `sideeye mcp`, and three skills (`npx skills@1.7.1 add yottayoshida/sideeye`): [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md). ## Writing the check The check, like the setup, receives the state directory in `$SIDEEYE_STATE_DIR`. This one cross-examines the tool's own diagnostic; the violation is the claim and the observable truth disagreeing: ```sh claim=$("$TOY" doctor 2>/dev/null) || claim="unhealthy" "$TOY" load-key >/dev/null 2>&1 && reality="loadable" || reality="unloadable" case "$claim:$reality" in healthy:loadable | unhealthy:unloadable) exit 0 ;; *) echo "doctor says '$claim' but the key is $reality" >&2; exit 1 ;; esac ``` Sideeye refuses to trust a checker it has not seen fail: it corrupts the state first. A checker that cannot fail makes the run UNKNOWN, not PASS; so does an exploration in which no world could have failed ([conditions](docs/report-schema.md)). ## What the target has to be Sideeye refuses to guess: outside these limits the verdict is UNKNOWN, naming the detector. Reasons: [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md#known-constraints-declared-not-hidden). - **Dynamically linked**, reaching files through libc; static only under `--observe supervised` (Linux). Hardened runtimes are refused. Threads are judged where a creation or a join the shim saw orders their writes. - **Under `--observe syscalls`, a process whose `SIGSYS` is blocked or reset dies at its first state-changing call** — an `exec`'d image the shim cannot reach, a `posix_spawn` child. - **Byte-repeatable writes** (`preflight --twice` checks), **state in one directory**, **a clean run exits its declared success status**. - **Other processes take turns with the state**, and every writing child is reaped; a process boundary needs Linux's `--oracle`, and one that leaves its process group is judged only where the engine can hold the run in a cgroup (Linux) — otherwise UNKNOWN. - **On macOS, a framework Python's `bin/python3` is a launcher**; Sideeye refuses it and names the interpreter to run instead. No language model decides a verdict; a PASS is a search record naming what was *not* tested. ## Documentation [docs/faq.md](docs/faq.md) · [docs/cli.md](docs/cli.md) · [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md) · [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) · [docs/report-schema.md](docs/report-schema.md) · [docs/target-classes.md](docs/target-classes.md) · [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) · [docs/](docs/) ## License [MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or [Apache-2.0](LICENSE-APACHE), at your option. # The CLI in full The README carries the shortest path to a first verdict.
